short: Theodosius banned pagan sacrifice and temple worship empire-wide, ending state paganism.
full:
In June 391, Theodosius issued a law to the urban prefect of Rome banning all sacrifice and forbidding anyone from entering a pagan temple, visiting shrines, or venerating statues, on pain of heavy fines. A parallel edict addressed to Alexandria followed in June 392, extending the ban across the eastern provinces and prompting riots in which the Serapeum, one of the ancient world's great pagan sanctuaries, was destroyed by a Christian mob.

Together the edicts went further than Constantine or his successors had dared, converting decades of preferential treatment for Christianity into the active suppression of traditional cult. Temples were closed, their endowments confiscated, and public funding for pagan priesthoods withdrawn across the empire. The laws did not eliminate private pagan belief, which persisted for generations, but they ended paganism's legal standing as a component of Roman civic life.
